prize_parts.citation: for showing how technology and import competition reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: B030 combines an explanatory framework (tasks, automation and polarisation) with newly assembled data and quasi-experimental identification (the import-competition shock and local labour-market adjustment). I weight that combination heavily, because new evidence together with a framework that explains it is what changes understanding. The work addresses a large question, it is hard to answer, and it has had real consequences for research and policy. It also pushed economists to take distributional costs and slow adjustment seriously instead of assuming frictionless reallocation. The China-shock design is a joint Autor-Dorn-Hanson contribution, and the task approach is Autor's. The three proposed names therefore map onto identifiable parts of the work. The literature is roughly two decades old, heavily replicated and extended, and it has stabilised around its main findings, with debate over magnitudes. It is also relevant to current discussion of automation and trade adjustment.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the credit is diffuse and the evidence is still being refined. The task framework has other authors (Levy and Murnane, Katz, and Acemoglu, who is already a laureate and is not on this ballot). The trade-shock and technology strands are distinct contributions, and a single citation risks blurring them. The persistence and magnitude of the China-shock effects, and shift-share identification, are actively debated. There is also some topical adjacency to the 2023 and 2024 prizes, and a three-person cap forces the exclusion of Katz.

responses.point: Peter ranks B030 seventh. He regards it as only moderately mature, with the long-run interpretation of the China shock and the shift-share methodology still debated, and he notes that credit is shared with Katz, Acemoglu and others.
responses.response: The shift-share concern is fair and I would not dismiss it. I read it as a debate about magnitudes and inference, not about whether the effects exist. The core finding of persistent local labour-market adjustment costs has been replicated and extended by other authors with other designs. I also think the credit problem is smaller for the China-shock strand than for the task framework. That is why my citation stresses technology and import competition together as drivers of labour demand, not a priority claim over the whole task literature. I accept Peter's point that maturity is lower here than for B005 or B014. I still think two decades of scrutiny is enough to judge lasting influence, but he is right that the persistence question is not fully settled.

responses.point: Timo ranks B030 second but proposes Autor, Hanson and Katz. He credits Katz with the skill-demand and education-race strand and treats Dorn as the most plausible omission. He also notes the debate over China-shock effects and the overlap with recent prizes.
responses.response: Timo and I agree on the scientific case and differ only on the third name. Katz's skill-bias and education-race work is foundational. But the achievement I would cite is the task framework together with the trade-shock evidence, and Dorn is a core co-author of the identification design in the China-shock papers. I also think the skill-bias and education-race strand sits close to the labour-and-history work recognised in 2023. I draw that link from general knowledge, since it is not in the supplied evidence. I therefore lean toward Dorn, though I see this as a real judgement call and not a clear-cut attribution. If the committee wanted the broader technology-and-skills framing, Katz's case would be stronger. That is a separate achievement from the one I propose.

responses.point: Tommy ranks B005 first. He argues that BLP demand estimation and dynamic industry models changed empirical industrial organisation and are standard in merger review and regulation. He names the main risks as a methods prize with no single headline finding, and the choice between Bresnahan, Reiss and Levinsohn.
responses.response: Tommy's case is serious and I have moved toward treating B005 as a live alternative. The breadth of use in antitrust, trade and health is a common criterion that I apply to my own candidate too. I did not rank B005 in my opening. That reflects my own background in labour and crime, not a judgement that the contribution is weaker, so I give extra weight to colleagues closer to that field. I still prefer B030 on two grounds. It answers a substantive question about who bears the costs of technological and trade change. The attribution of the BLP core is clean, but the three-name boundary Tommy describes (Levinsohn versus Bresnahan or Reiss) is less clean than in the B030 trio. I would not be unhappy if the committee concluded that methodological reach should outweigh substantive findings.

responses.point: Kerstin ranks B030 fourth. She values the persistent local effects and the policy relevance but worries about overlap with the 2024 and 2025 prizes. She also asks whether the task framework should be credited mainly to others, such as Acemoglu.
responses.response: I take the Acemoglu point seriously, and it is why I would anchor the citation in empirical demonstration and the labour-demand framework. Autor's task-based work with Levy and Murnane, and his later trade-shock work, are independent of the institutions work recognised in 2024. On topical overlap, I do not think adjacency to a recent prize is evidence against a contribution, since the common test is the specific scientific contribution. I agree that the committee should check whether the technology strand and the trade strand together make one prize or two separate ones. If it judges they do not fit together, the China-shock work alone is the stronger-attributed piece.

uncertainties: Whether Dorn or Katz is the better third name, given the overlap of Katz's skill-bias work with prior recognition. My view of that overlap is not independently verified.
How far the persistence and magnitude debate on China-shock effects, and shift-share identification, should lower the weight on maturity.
Whether the technology (tasks) and trade-shock strands form one coherent prize motivation or should be treated as separate achievements.
Whether the committee would give more weight to the breadth of methodological use in B005 than to the substantive findings in B030. My own field proximity may bias me toward B030.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile as a co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Hanson, Dorn or the other credited names. My frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not on the shortlist. I do work in labour economics, so there is field proximity to B030, B001 and B009, which I disclose without adjudicating.
